title: AML/CFT Compliance Professional
tagline: Follow the money, spot the risk and report it right: practical AML, CFT and sanctions compliance for Pakistan's financial sector.
description:
Every account you open, every remittance you pay and every trade document you check is a point where criminals and terrorist financiers try to get in. This certification builds the judgement that front-line and compliance staff need to keep them out, and to stay on the right side of Pakistan's law and its regulators.

You will learn how money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing actually work, how the **FATF standards** and **Pakistan's framework** (the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010, the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997, the Financial Monitoring Unit, SBP and SECP regulations) fit together, and why Pakistan's grey-list years still shape supervision today.

The course is built around practice, not theory: risk-rating real-looking customers, unwrapping ownership structures, reviewing PEP and NPO relationships, investigating alerts, spotting trade-based laundering, writing a strong suspicious transaction report without tipping off the customer, and handling a sanctions match from first alert to freeze.

Five stages, ten-question tests after each, and a tough timed final exam built from realistic Pakistani scenarios.
audience: Branch, operations and customer-service staff in banks and microfinance banks who open accounts and handle cash
Compliance, AML and sanctions analysts who review alerts, PEPs and high-risk customers
Trade finance, remittance and treasury staff who process cross-border payments
Staff of exchange companies, insurers, brokers, fintechs and payment service providers
Real estate agents, jewellers, accountants and other DNFBPs with AML/CFT obligations
Internal auditors and risk managers who test AML/CFT controls
outcomes: Explain how money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing work and how FATF and Pakistan's laws respond to them
Apply the risk-based approach to rate customers, products, geographies and channels and to justify the result
Perform customer due diligence, identify beneficial owners and decide when simplified or enhanced measures apply
Recognise red flags in branches, trade, remittances and digital channels and investigate alerts in a disciplined way
Escalate and report suspicions correctly, write a clear STR narrative and avoid tipping off
Screen against UN and domestic lists and act on a true match by freezing and reporting without delay
Describe the parts of an effective compliance programme and the consequences when it fails

quest.name: Follow the Rupee
quest.premise: You have just joined the financial crime desk of a mid-sized Pakistani bank. On your first morning, the Chief Compliance Officer, Ayesha Siddiqui, hands you a file: a trail of cash deposits in Multan, wallet transfers in Karachi, an export invoice from Faisalabad and a remittance from the Gulf that all seem to connect. Five stages stand between you and the truth. Master each one, then face the final boss: presenting your case to the bank's board.

sessions.title: Dirty Money, Terror Funds and the Rules of the Game
sessions.summary: Before you can follow the money, you need the map: how laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing work, why they matter to Pakistan, and which international standards, laws and authorities shape your obligations.
objectives: Describe the three stages of money laundering and recognise them in Pakistani scenarios
Distinguish terrorist financing and proliferation financing from money laundering
Explain the role of FATF, its Recommendations and mutual evaluations, and Pakistan's grey-list history
Map Pakistan's AML/CFT laws and the roles of the FMU, SBP, SECP and other supervisors

cards.title: Money laundering: making dirty money look clean
cards.body:
**Money laundering** is the process of disguising the criminal origin of money or property so that it can be used without raising suspicion. The underlying crime is called the **predicate offence**: corruption, drug trafficking, smuggling, fraud, kidnapping for ransom, tax evasion and many others. Laundering is a separate crime from the predicate offence, and in Pakistan a person can be prosecuted for both.

Laundering is traditionally explained in three stages:

- **Placement**: getting criminal proceeds, often cash, into the financial system. Examples: cash deposits split across several accounts, buying prize bonds or gold with cash, mixing illegal cash with the takings of a genuine cash business such as a petrol pump or a wholesale shop.
- **Layering**: moving the money through many transactions to break the audit trail. Examples: rapid transfers between accounts of relatives and front companies, round-tripping through foreign accounts, trade payments against inflated invoices, buying and selling assets quickly.
- **Integration**: bringing the money back into the legitimate economy so it looks like ordinary wealth. Examples: buying plots and houses, investing in a business, 'loans' from a company the criminal secretly controls.

The stages are a model, not a rulebook. Real cases skip stages, run them at the same time, or start at layering because the proceeds are already in a bank (fraud and corruption proceeds often are). Your job is not to label the stage perfectly; it is to notice when a customer's activity has no sensible economic purpose and could be hiding where the money came from.

cards.title: Terrorist financing and proliferation financing
cards.body:
**Terrorist financing (TF)** is providing or collecting funds or other assets, by any means, for terrorist acts, terrorist organisations or individual terrorists, even when no specific attack is linked to the money. Two features make it different from laundering:

- **The source can be legitimate.** Donations, business profits, salaries or charitable collections can be diverted to terrorism. The focus is on where the money is going, not only on where it came from.
- **Amounts are often small.** A few thousand rupees through a wallet, a modest monthly transfer or a cash courier can be enough. Large-value thresholds will not catch it; behaviour and connections will.

Common TF methods in the region include fundraising under the cover of charity or religious causes, use of front organisations after a group is banned, cash couriers, unlicensed hawala and hundi, and small transfers through mobile wallets.

**Proliferation financing (PF)** is providing funds or financial services that support the development, acquisition or transfer of nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their delivery systems, in breach of national law or UN Security Council obligations. PF usually hides inside trade: dual-use goods (items with both civilian and weapons uses), front companies, false end-user declarations and indirect shipping routes.

| | ML | TF | PF |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main question | Where did it come from? | Where is it going? | What will it buy, for whom? |
| Source | Criminal | Legal or criminal | Usually commercial |
| Typical size | Often large | Often small | Varies, trade-linked |

FATF expects countries and institutions to address all three, and Pakistan's regulations now refer to **AML/CFT/CPF** for that reason.

cards.title: The ghee distributor who bought too many plots
cards.body:
Kashif runs a ghee and cooking oil distribution business in Faisalabad with a turnover that his bank profiles at about PKR 15 million a month. Over six months, his branch notices a change.

**What happened:**

1. Cash deposits of PKR 400,000 to 900,000 start arriving almost daily, made by different people at branches in Faisalabad, Sargodha and Jhang. None of the depositors are known employees.
2. Within a day or two, most of each deposit is transferred to the accounts of three newly registered 'trading' firms. Two of them share an address with Kashif's warehouse.
3. The trading firms pay a property dealer in Lahore and a car showroom, and one of them sends payments abroad against invoices for 'edible oil machinery' that never appears in import records.
4. Kashif then buys four residential plots in a gated housing scheme, describing the money as 'business profit'.

**Mapping the stages:**

- **Placement:** third-party cash deposits in several cities, mixed into a genuine cash business so they look like sales receipts.
- **Layering:** quick transfers to related front firms and payments against questionable invoices, which break the link between the cash and its source.
- **Integration:** plots and vehicles that now look like the fruits of a successful business.

**What the bank should notice:** deposits far above the profile, deposited by unrelated people in other cities, money that passes straight through, new related firms with no clear business, and trade payments without matching goods. No single fact proves a crime. Together they make a strong case for internal escalation and, after review, a suspicious transaction report. The investigation of the underlying crime is the job of law enforcement, not the bank.

cards.question: A government officer receives bribes directly into his salary account, then buys a commercial shop in his cousin's name with a pay order from that account. Which statement best describes this?
options: It cannot be laundering because the money entered the bank openly in the officer's own name
It is laundering: the proceeds were already in the system, and using a relative's name to buy property disguises ownership
It is only a corruption case; laundering requires cash and a foreign transfer
It is laundering only if the shop is later sold at a profit
cards.explanation: Laundering does not require cash or a foreign leg. Corruption proceeds often enter the bank directly, so placement is skipped, and putting the asset in a relative's name disguises true ownership, which is classic layering and integration. Depositing in his own name does not make the money clean.

cards.title: Why it matters: country, institution and you
cards.body:
AML/CFT is sometimes treated as paperwork. The consequences of getting it wrong show why it is not.

**For Pakistan:** when a country is judged to have serious weaknesses, FATF places it under increased monitoring (the 'grey list'). Foreign banks then apply extra checks to its transactions, correspondent relationships become harder to keep, trade and remittance costs rise and investors become cautious. Pakistan experienced this directly between 2018 and 2022. Weak controls also let corruption, smuggling and terrorism flourish, which harms ordinary citizens long before any rating changes.

**For your institution:** regulators can impose monetary penalties, restrict business, require remediation programmes and act against senior management. Foreign correspondent banks may close relationships with an institution they consider poorly controlled, which can cut off trade finance and remittances. Reputational damage from being named in a terrorism or corruption case can last years.

**For you personally:** the law places obligations on individuals, not only on institutions. Knowingly assisting laundering is itself an offence. Telling a customer that a report has been or may be filed (tipping off) is an offence. Staff who ignore obvious red flags, override controls for a valued client or backdate records can face disciplinary action, regulatory action and, in serious cases, prosecution.

The flip side is important too. Good-faith reporting is protected by law, and well-documented decisions protect staff. A clear file note that explains what you saw and why you escalated is one of the best protections you will ever have.

cards.title: The international framework: FATF and its standards
cards.body:
The **Financial Action Task Force (FATF)** is an inter-governmental body set up by the G7 in 1989. It sets the global standards for fighting money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing and checks whether countries meet them.

**The FATF Recommendations** (40 in total, comprehensively revised in 2012 and updated many times since) cover, among other things:

- national risk assessment and the risk-based approach
- criminalising ML and TF, and confiscating proceeds
- targeted financial sanctions for TF and PF
- preventive measures for financial institutions and DNFBPs: customer due diligence, record keeping, PEPs, correspondent banking, wire transfers, new technologies, internal controls and suspicious transaction reporting
- transparency of beneficial ownership of companies and trusts
- powers of supervisors, financial intelligence units and law enforcement, and international cooperation

**Mutual evaluations** are peer reviews. Assessors rate **technical compliance** (are the laws and rules in place?) and **effectiveness** (are they actually working?), the latter measured against 11 Immediate Outcomes. A country can have good laws on paper and still be rated ineffective if, for example, few STRs lead to investigations or sanctions are never applied.

Most countries are assessed by a **FATF-style regional body**. Pakistan is a member of the **Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG)**. Countries with serious deficiencies may be publicly identified: jurisdictions under increased monitoring (the grey list) work through an agreed action plan, while high-risk jurisdictions subject to a call for action (often called the black list) face countermeasures.

Other building blocks include UN conventions on drugs, organised crime, corruption and terrorist financing, UN Security Council sanctions resolutions, and the **Egmont Group**, the network through which financial intelligence units share information.

cards.title: Pakistan's grey-list journey and what it taught
cards.body:
Pakistan has been on FATF's list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring more than once. It was listed between 2012 and 2015, and was placed on the list again in **June 2018**, mainly over terrorist financing risks.

**The action plans.** In 2018 Pakistan committed to a 27-item action plan focused on TF: understanding TF risk, supervising institutions, freezing assets of designated persons, prosecuting TF and controlling cash couriers and unlicensed money transfer. After the APG mutual evaluation adopted in 2019 identified wider weaknesses, a second action plan with 7 further items, focused mainly on money laundering, was agreed in 2021.

**The reforms.** Between 2019 and 2022 Pakistan amended its AML, anti-terrorism and UN sanctions laws, strengthened supervision by SBP and SECP, brought DNFBPs such as real estate agents and jewellers under AML/CFT supervision, increased TF investigations and convictions, and tightened action against unlicensed hawala and hundi. Supervisors issued heavier penalties, and institutions overhauled screening, CDD and reporting.

**The exit.** After FATF judged both action plans substantially complete and an on-site visit confirmed progress, Pakistan was removed from increased monitoring in **October 2022**.

**The lesson for practitioners.** Exit came from evidence of effectiveness: STRs that led to cases, freezes that happened without delay, penalties that were actually imposed. Those expectations did not end in 2022. Future mutual evaluations will again test whether the system works in practice, which means whether staff like you identify customers properly, report quality STRs and act on sanctions lists without hesitation.

cards.title: Grey-list exit is not a finish line
cards.body: You will hear colleagues say 'we are off the grey list now, so things can relax'. They cannot. Removal reflects what Pakistan had already achieved; the next mutual evaluation will measure what the system is achieving then. Supervisors continue to inspect, penalise and publish enforcement actions. Treat every control as if an assessor will sample your file, because one day they may.

cards.title: Pakistan's legal framework
cards.body:
Several laws work together. You do not need to memorise section numbers, but you must know what each law does.

**Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 (AMLA), as amended.** The core AML law. It:

- criminalises money laundering and links it to a schedule of predicate offences
- establishes the **Financial Monitoring Unit (FMU)** as Pakistan's financial intelligence unit
- places preventive obligations on **reporting entities** (financial institutions and DNFBPs): customer due diligence, record keeping, reporting suspicious and currency transactions, and a ban on tipping off
- gives supervisors powers to regulate and sanction reporting entities, and protects good-faith reporting from liability

Major amendments in 2020 strengthened penalties, expanded supervision to DNFBPs and gave supervisors stronger enforcement powers.

**Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997 (ATA).** The main law for **terrorist financing**. It criminalises raising, using and possessing funds for terrorism, provides for the proscription of organisations and persons, and requires freezing of the funds and property of those proscribed.

**United Nations (Security Council) Act, 1948.** The legal basis through which the federal government gives effect to UN Security Council sanctions, including asset freezes on designated persons, by issuing statutory orders.

**Regulations made under these laws.** SBP's AML/CFT/CPF Regulations for the institutions it supervises, SECP's AML/CFT regulations for its regulated persons, and the rules applied to DNFBPs by their supervisors turn the law into detailed, enforceable requirements.

Other laws matter too, including foreign exchange law (relevant to unlicensed hawala and hundi), customs law (cash smuggling and trade fraud) and export control law (proliferation-sensitive goods).

cards.title: Who does what: FMU, supervisors and law enforcement
cards.body:
Knowing the roles helps you understand where your report goes and who can ask you for records.

| Body | Main role |
|---|---|
| **Financial Monitoring Unit (FMU)** | Pakistan's FIU. Receives STRs and CTRs, analyses them, disseminates financial intelligence to law enforcement, issues guidance and red-flag indicators, and cooperates with foreign FIUs |
| **State Bank of Pakistan (SBP)** | Regulator and AML/CFT supervisor for banks, microfinance banks, DFIs, exchange companies and payment and e-money institutions it licenses. Issues the AML/CFT/CPF Regulations, inspects and imposes penalties |
| **Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP)** | Supervisor for securities brokers, insurers, NBFCs, modarabas and other entities it regulates; also maintains company and beneficial ownership information |
| **DNFBP supervisors** | Bodies designated to supervise real estate agents, dealers in precious metals and stones, accountants and other DNFBPs |
| **Law enforcement agencies** | Investigate and prosecute ML, TF and predicate crimes, for example FIA, NAB, ANF, Customs, provincial Counter Terrorism Departments and tax authorities |

Two points often confuse staff.

- **The FMU is not your supervisor.** It is the intelligence hub that receives your reports. SBP or SECP checks whether you complied.
- **The FMU does not investigate crimes itself.** It analyses information and passes intelligence to the agencies that do.

Any request from a law enforcement agency for customer records should go through your compliance function, which checks that it has proper legal authority before information is shared.

cards.title: One remittance, many authorities
cards.body:
Rabia Anwar works at the counter of an exchange company in Peshawar that SBP licenses and that pays out inward home remittances. A customer, Mr Durrani, comes to collect about PKR 1.3 million sent from Dubai. Rabia identifies him with his CNIC and completes biometric verification.

Over the next month, Mr Durrani returns three times to collect similar amounts, each from a different sender in a different Gulf city. His stated occupation is a shopkeeper with modest income. One of the senders' names closely resembles a name in a press report about a banned outfit's fundraising.

Follow the responsibilities:

- **Rabia and the exchange company** must apply CDD, screen the customer and the senders against sanctions and proscription lists, notice that the pattern does not fit the customer's profile, and escalate internally. They must not hint to Mr Durrani that he is under suspicion.
- **The compliance officer** reviews the case, checks whether the name match is a true match, and if suspicion remains files an **STR with the FMU**. If a true match to a designated or proscribed person is confirmed, the company must **freeze** and report in line with the current TFS instructions.
- **SBP**, as supervisor, will later inspect whether the company's CDD, screening and reporting worked, and can penalise failures.
- **The FMU** analyses the STR, links it with other reports, and if warranted passes intelligence to the relevant **Counter Terrorism Department** or **FIA**, which may investigate.

One transaction, five sets of responsibilities. The front-line step, noticing and escalating, is what makes the rest possible.

cards.question: Which statement about Pakistan's Financial Monitoring Unit (FMU) is correct?
options: It is the prudential supervisor of banks and imposes penalties for weak KYC
It is the financial intelligence unit that receives and analyses STRs and CTRs and disseminates intelligence
It prosecutes money laundering cases in the banking courts
It licenses exchange companies and approves their compliance officers
cards.explanation: The FMU is Pakistan's FIU: it receives, analyses and disseminates financial intelligence. Supervising, licensing and penalising banks and exchange companies is SBP's role, and investigation and prosecution belong to law enforcement agencies and prosecutors.

cards.question: Why do high-value transaction thresholds often fail to detect terrorist financing?
options: Because TF transactions are always in foreign currency
Because TF can involve small amounts from legitimate sources, so behaviour and connections matter more than size
Because TF is only reported through CTRs, not STRs
Because terrorist groups never use the formal banking system
cards.explanation: TF frequently uses small amounts and may start from legitimate funds such as donations or salaries. Size-based rules miss it; patterns, counterparties and links to proscribed or designated persons are the stronger indicators. Terrorist groups do use banks, wallets and exchange companies.

cards.title: Build your own source library
cards.body: Rules change through new regulations, circulars, FAQs and list updates. Do not rely on old training slides or a colleague's memory. Keep bookmarks to the official websites of **SBP**, the **FMU**, **SECP**, **NACTA** and the **Ministry of Foreign Affairs**, and ask your compliance team how updates are circulated internally. When this course says 'check the latest instructions', that is a real step in your job, not a disclaimer.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: Money laundering disguises the criminal origin of assets; placement, layering and integration are a model, and real cases often skip or overlap stages.
Terrorist financing is about where money is going: it can be small and come from legitimate sources. Proliferation financing usually hides in trade.
FATF sets the standards; mutual evaluations test both laws and effectiveness. Pakistan is assessed through the APG.
Pakistan was on the grey list from June 2018 until October 2022; exit required proof that controls work, and that expectation continues.
AMLA 2010 covers ML and reporting duties, ATA 1997 covers TF and proscription, and the UN (Security Council) Act 1948 gives effect to UN sanctions.
The FMU receives and analyses reports; SBP and SECP supervise; law enforcement investigates and prosecutes.

cards.prompt: Think of the products and services your own team handles. At which point could a criminal or terrorist financier most easily get money into, through or out of your institution, and who on your team would be the first to notice?

quiz.question: A wholesale cloth trader in Karachi mixes cash from smuggled goods with his genuine daily shop takings and deposits the total each evening. Which stage of money laundering does this most clearly represent?
options: Integration, because once mixed into a legitimate business the money already looks like ordinary trading income
Placement, because criminal cash is entering the financial system disguised as business receipts
Layering, because mixing criminal cash with genuine takings is itself the step that breaks the audit trail
None, because the trader runs a real business
quiz.explanation: Depositing criminal cash mixed with genuine takings is placement: the proceeds enter the banking system looking like sales. Layering involves moving funds through further transactions to break the trail. A genuine business can still be used to launder.

quiz.question: Which feature most clearly distinguishes terrorist financing from money laundering?
options: Terrorist financing always involves cross-border wire transfers
Terrorist financing is only committed by proscribed organisations, not individuals
Terrorist financing requires the funds to have been used in a completed attack before any offence or report arises
Terrorist financing can use funds from legitimate sources, because the concern is their destination
quiz.explanation: TF is defined by the purpose of the funds, so donations, salaries and business profits can all be TF. It does not require a completed attack, can be committed by any individual, and frequently uses domestic channels.

quiz.question: In a FATF mutual evaluation, what does an 'effectiveness' rating measure?
options: How well the country's AML/CFT system achieves results in practice, assessed against Immediate Outcomes
Whether the country has enacted the laws, regulations and enforceable measures needed to cover each FATF Recommendation
The number of banks that have adopted automated monitoring systems
Whether the country has paid its contributions to its FATF-style regional body and attended plenary meetings regularly
quiz.explanation: Effectiveness measures whether the system delivers results in practice, for example investigations, convictions, freezes and quality supervision, against 11 Immediate Outcomes. Whether laws exist on paper is technical compliance, a separate rating.

quiz.question: Which statement about Pakistan's most recent period on FATF's list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring is accurate?
options: Pakistan was listed in 2015 and removed in 2018 after completing a single action plan focused on terrorist financing
Pakistan was placed on the call-for-action list in 2018 and faced countermeasures from FATF members until 2022
Pakistan was listed in June 2018 and removed in October 2022 after completing two action plans
Pakistan was listed in 2020 because of proliferation financing concerns only
quiz.explanation: Pakistan was grey-listed in June 2018 and removed in October 2022 after completing the 2018 TF-focused action plan and the 2021 ML-focused action plan. It was under increased monitoring (grey list), not on the call-for-action (black) list.

quiz.question: A trading company imports 'industrial vacuum pumps' through a free-trade hub for an end user whose identity keeps changing, and payment comes from an unrelated third party. Which risk does this pattern raise most directly?
options: Tax evasion through customs undervaluation only
Proliferation financing, because the goods may be dual-use and the end user is unclear
Terrorist financing, because third-party payments routed through a free-trade hub are the most common TF method
Market manipulation in the securities market
quiz.explanation: Dual-use goods, indirect routing, an unclear end user and third-party payment are classic proliferation financing indicators. Nothing suggests small amounts or terrorism links, and undervaluation alone would not explain the changing end user.

quiz.question: Which law is Pakistan's main legal basis for criminalising terrorist financing and for proscribing organisations and persons?
options: The Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997
The Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010
The United Nations (Security Council) Act, 1948
The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947
quiz.explanation: The ATA 1997 criminalises TF and provides for proscription of organisations and persons with related freezing. AMLA covers money laundering and reporting duties; the UN (Security Council) Act gives effect to UN sanctions; foreign exchange law addresses matters such as unlicensed money transfer.

quiz.question: Sunil, a branch officer, receives a call from someone claiming to be from a law enforcement agency asking for a customer's statement 'urgently, by WhatsApp'. What should he do?
options: Send the statement promptly, because law enforcement agencies have legal powers to obtain records and delay could obstruct them
Refuse permanently, because customer records can never be shared with any authority
Ask the caller to email the FMU, since only the FMU can request records
Route the request to the compliance function so it can verify the legal authority before anything is shared
quiz.explanation: Authorities can lawfully obtain records, but staff must not share data on an unverified informal request. Compliance checks the requester's identity and legal authority and responds through proper channels. Refusing every request is wrong, and the FMU is not the only body with access powers.

quiz.question: Which body supervises a licensed exchange company in Pakistan for AML/CFT compliance?
options: The Financial Monitoring Unit
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan
The State Bank of Pakistan
The Federal Board of Revenue
quiz.explanation: Exchange companies are licensed and supervised by SBP. The FMU receives their reports but is not their supervisor; SECP supervises securities, insurance and NBFC sectors; FBR's DNFBP role relates to sectors such as real estate and precious metals dealers.

quiz.question: A senior colleague says: 'Since Pakistan left the grey list in 2022, supervisors will focus on prudential issues and AML inspections will ease.' What is the best response?
options: Agree, because FATF only reviews countries that are on a public list
Disagree: future mutual evaluations will test effectiveness again, and supervisors continue AML/CFT inspections and penalties
Agree partly: after exit only terrorist financing controls remain a supervisory focus, since the action plans were TF-driven
Disagree, because Pakistan is still on the grey list under a new action plan
quiz.explanation: All countries undergo periodic mutual evaluations whether or not they are listed, and effectiveness will be tested again. Supervision and enforcement continue. Pakistan was removed in October 2022, so the claim that it remains listed is wrong, and ML controls matter as much as TF controls.

quiz.question: Why does FATF's assessment of a country look at both technical compliance and effectiveness?
options: Because effectiveness only applies to countries already on the grey list
Because technical compliance covers financial institutions while effectiveness covers only law enforcement
Because a country can have sound laws that are not applied in practice, so real-world results must also be tested
Because technical compliance is assessed by the FIU and effectiveness by the central bank
quiz.explanation: Laws on paper do not guarantee outcomes. FATF separately checks whether the framework produces results, such as quality STRs, investigations, confiscation and supervision. Both ratings apply to every assessed country and are made by the assessment team, not by domestic agencies.

sessions.title: The Risk-Based Approach: Seeing Where the Danger Lies
sessions.summary: From the watchtower you see the whole landscape. Learn how institutions assess their ML/TF/PF risk, how customer, product, geography and channel factors combine into a risk rating, and how ratings drive the controls you apply.
objectives: Explain the risk-based approach, inherent risk, controls and residual risk
Describe the steps of an enterprise-wide risk assessment and how it links to Pakistan's national risk assessment
Assess customer, product/service, geographic and delivery channel risk factors
Assign and justify customer risk ratings and explain what each rating triggers
Distinguish sound risk management from wholesale de-risking

cards.title: What the risk-based approach really means
cards.body:
No institution can check every customer and transaction with maximum intensity. The **risk-based approach (RBA)**, the first of the FATF Recommendations, asks countries and institutions to understand their ML/TF/PF risks and to put stronger controls where risks are higher and simpler controls where they are genuinely lower.

Three ideas sit at its heart:

- **Inherent risk**: the risk that exists before any controls, arising from who your customers are, what you sell, where you operate and how you deliver services.
- **Controls**: the measures that reduce risk, such as CDD, screening, transaction monitoring, limits, approvals, training and audit.
- **Residual risk**: the risk that remains after controls. It should fall within the institution's **risk appetite**, approved by the board.

A simple way to think about any risk is **threat x vulnerability x consequence**. The threat is the criminal or terrorist intent (for example, drug proceeds from a smuggling route). The vulnerability is the weakness they could exploit (for example, a cash-heavy branch with weak monitoring). The consequence is the harm if they succeed.

What the RBA is **not**:

- It is not permission to do less. Lower-risk treatment must be justified by evidence, and some requirements apply whatever the rating, such as sanctions screening and reporting suspicion.
- It is not zero tolerance. The goal is to manage risk sensibly, not to eliminate every customer who carries some risk.
- It is not a one-time exercise. Risks change with new products, new typologies and new national findings, and the assessment must keep up.

Regulators in Pakistan expect institutions to be able to **show their working**: what risks they identified, how they rated them, what they did about them and why.

cards.title: The enterprise-wide risk assessment
cards.body:
Before rating individual customers, an institution must understand its risk as a whole. This is the **enterprise-wide (or institutional) risk assessment**. SBP and SECP expect it to be documented, approved at senior level and kept up to date.

**A practical sequence:**

1. **Gather data.** Numbers and types of customers, high-risk segments, PEPs, NPOs, non-resident customers, product volumes, cash intensity, cross-border flows by country, channel usage, STR and alert statistics, audit and inspection findings.
2. **Use external inputs.** Pakistan's **national risk assessment** identifies major threats such as corruption, drug trafficking, smuggling, tax crimes, fraud, unlicensed hawala and hundi, and terrorist financing linked to proscribed groups. Add FATF and FMU typologies and sector risk assessments.
3. **Assess inherent risk** for each risk category: customers, products and services, geographies, and delivery channels. Assess TF and **proliferation financing** risk explicitly; FATF requires PF risk to be assessed as well.
4. **Assess control effectiveness.** Do the controls exist, and do they work? Use evidence from testing, audit and quality assurance, not assumptions.
5. **Determine residual risk** and compare it with the board-approved risk appetite.
6. **Act.** Where residual risk is too high, strengthen controls, limit products, exit segments or add resources, with owners and deadlines.
7. **Approve, communicate and refresh.** Present results to senior management and the board, share relevant parts with business lines, and update periodically and whenever something material changes, such as a new product, a new country corridor, a new national risk finding or a major incident.

The enterprise assessment shapes everything else: the customer risk model, monitoring scenarios, training priorities and audit plans. If it is a copy-paste document that nobody uses, those downstream controls will drift away from real risk.

cards.title: Customer risk factors
cards.body:
Customer risk is usually the most important driver of a rating. Consider several kinds of factor together.

**Who the customer is**

- Politically exposed persons, their family members and close associates
- Non-profit organisations, especially those operating in conflict-affected or high-risk areas
- Non-resident customers and those whose identity is hard to verify
- Legal persons with complex, layered or opaque ownership, or nominee arrangements
- Customers with relevant adverse media, past STRs or links to proscribed persons

**What the customer does**

- Cash-intensive businesses: wholesale markets, petrol pumps, used-car dealers, real estate dealers, jewellers and gold traders
- Businesses exposed to trade risk: import-export, especially of goods that are easy to mis-price or that may be dual-use
- Money service businesses and agents
- Occupations with access to public funds or procurement decisions

**How the customer behaves**

- Reluctance to provide information, inconsistent explanations, frequent changes of details
- Activity out of line with stated income or business
- Use of many accounts or third parties without a clear reason

**Lower-risk indicators** can include salaried employees of known employers whose activity matches their salary, government entities, listed companies subject to disclosure rules, and basic-tier accounts with strict limits.

Remember that no single factor makes a customer guilty. A jeweller is not a criminal because he is a jeweller. The factor tells you to look more carefully and to understand the business properly, not to assume the worst.

cards.title: Product, geography and channel risk
cards.body:
**Products and services** carry different vulnerabilities:

| Higher risk features | Examples |
|---|---|
| Cash in large amounts | Cash deposits, cash-funded remittances, currency exchange |
| Cross-border movement | Wire transfers, home remittances, trade finance, correspondent banking |
| Anonymity or third-party use | Bearer instruments, prepaid cards, wallets with weak KYC tiers |
| Speed and volume | Instant payments, high-limit digital transfers |
| Complexity | Private banking, structured products, trade finance with intermediaries |

**Geography** includes both foreign and domestic exposure. Foreign risk considers countries on FATF's lists, countries subject to UN sanctions, countries with high corruption or drug production, tax secrecy havens and conflict zones. Domestic risk considers areas identified in national assessments as exposed to smuggling, cross-border cash movement or terrorist activity. Use geography carefully: it should raise attention, not lead to automatic refusal of everyone from a district.

**Delivery channels** describe how the customer reaches you:

- **Face to face** at a branch with biometric verification is generally lower risk.
- **Non-face-to-face** onboarding through apps and digital channels can be well controlled with strong digital identity checks, but carries impersonation and mule risks.
- **Agents and intermediaries** such as branchless banking agents, insurance agents and introducers add risk because you rely on someone else's diligence and integrity.

These categories interact. A low-risk customer using a high-risk product through a high-risk channel to a high-risk country may need far more attention than any single factor suggests. Good risk models combine factors rather than looking at each in isolation.

cards.title: Rating three customers in Gujranwala
cards.body:
Hamza Latif, a compliance analyst, reviews three new relationships at a Gujranwala branch using the bank's scoring model (1 = low, 3 = high per factor).

| Factor | Scrap metal dealer | Software freelancer | Local education trust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Customer type | 3 (cash-intensive, many unbanked suppliers) | 1 (individual, salaried history) | 2 (NPO) |
| Product | 2 (current account, cash, pay orders) | 2 (foreign inward remittances) | 2 (current account, donations) |
| Geography | 1 (local) | 2 (payments from several countries) | 1 (local schools only) |
| Channel | 1 (branch) | 2 (mobile app) | 1 (branch) |
| **Result** | **High** (customer factor drives it) | **Medium** | **Medium** |

**Hamza's reasoning:**

- The **scrap dealer** is rated high because of heavy cash and payments to many unidentified suppliers, a recognised channel for laundering and tax evasion. The bank can still bank him, with enhanced due diligence: a site visit, supplier and buyer information, expected monthly cash volumes and closer monitoring.
- The **freelancer** receives payments from overseas platforms. That is normal for Pakistan's IT freelancing sector, but Hamza checks the platform names, invoices and that the volumes fit the work described.
- The **education trust** is an NPO, but it runs three local schools, publishes accounts and its trustees screen clean. Hamza rates it medium rather than high, records why, and sets a review if it starts receiving foreign donations or operating in new areas.

The point is not the arithmetic. It is that each rating can be explained and leads to proportionate action.

cards.question: A bank's assessment shows high inherent risk in its remittance business, but strong screening, limits and monitoring that are tested regularly. What should the assessment record?
options: That inherent risk is now low because controls are strong
High inherent risk, with residual risk reduced by tested controls and compared with risk appetite
Low residual risk only, because inherent risk does not need to be recorded
High residual risk, because controls never reduce risk in remittances
cards.explanation: Inherent risk is assessed before controls and does not change because controls are good. Effective, tested controls reduce residual risk, which is then compared with the board's risk appetite. Both must be recorded so the logic is visible.

cards.title: From rating to action
cards.body:
A risk rating is only useful if it changes what happens next. A typical framework links each rating to a set of measures:

| Rating | Typical measures |
|---|---|
| **Low** | Simplified due diligence where regulations allow, standard monitoring, longer review cycle |
| **Medium** | Standard CDD, standard monitoring, periodic review |
| **High** | Enhanced due diligence, senior management or compliance approval, source of funds and often source of wealth, tighter monitoring thresholds, more frequent reviews |

**Review frequency** is commonly set by rating, for example high-risk customers reviewed more often than low-risk ones. Your institution's policy will set the exact cycle; check it rather than assuming.

**Ratings must be dynamic.** Re-rate when a trigger occurs, not only at the scheduled review:

- the customer becomes a PEP or a PEP's associate
- adverse media or law enforcement enquiries appear
- an STR is filed or alerts repeat
- activity changes sharply: new countries, new products, much higher cash
- ownership or control of a company changes

**Overrides.** Models are blunt tools, so analysts may sometimes override a score. Overrides should be rare, documented with reasons and approved at an appropriate level. Downgrading a customer to avoid EDD workload, or because a relationship manager insists the client is 'very respectable', is a serious control failure that inspectors look for.

**Unacceptable risk.** Some customers fall outside risk appetite altogether: shell banks, anonymous accounts, persons designated under sanctions, or customers whose identity cannot be verified. These are not 'high risk'; they are not accepted.

cards.title: Watch for 'rating drift'
cards.body: In many inspections, the problem is not the model but how it is used. Common findings include: high-risk customers left at medium because a field was left blank, PEP status not updated after an election, business customers rated on the owner's profile rather than the business, and overrides with no reason recorded. Before you save a rating, ask yourself: **could I explain this rating to an inspector in two sentences, using what is on file?**

cards.title: A fintech launches a QR merchant wallet
cards.body:
A Karachi-based payment fintech licensed by SBP plans to launch a merchant wallet: small shopkeepers sign up through an app, display a QR code and receive instant payments from customers' bank and wallet accounts. The product team wants to launch in six weeks.

Zainab Tariq, the head of compliance, insists on a **product risk assessment before launch**, as FATF expects for new products and technologies.

**Risks she identifies:**

- Merchants onboarded remotely could be fake shops or **money mules** used to collect fraud proceeds.
- Instant settlement means stolen funds can leave within minutes.
- Agents paid per sign-up have an incentive to onboard anyone.
- Some merchants may operate in sectors linked to illegal gambling or unlicensed money transfer.

**Controls agreed:**

- Tiered onboarding: biometric or NADRA-backed identity checks for every merchant, with low limits until business proof and a location check are completed.
- Device and SIM checks to detect many wallets on one device.
- Monitoring scenarios for incoming payments far above shop size, many small payers who are new to the merchant, and rapid cash-out.
- Agent monitoring and clawback of commissions for fraudulent sign-ups.
- Sanctions and proscription screening at onboarding and on list updates.

**Outcome:** the launch moves by three weeks, the limits start conservative, and the assessment is approved by senior management with a review after three months of live data. The product is not refused; it is designed to be safe.

cards.title: Risk management, not de-risking
cards.body:
**De-risking** is when institutions refuse or end relationships with whole categories of customers, such as all NPOs, all exchange companies or everyone from a particular region, to avoid risk rather than to manage it.

FATF has repeatedly warned that wholesale de-risking is **not** what the risk-based approach requires. It can:

- push people and businesses into unregulated channels such as hawala and hundi, where nobody monitors anything
- undermine financial inclusion, which matters a great deal in Pakistan, where many adults have historically been unbanked
- harm legitimate charities doing humanitarian work
- reduce the information available to the FMU and law enforcement

The right approach is **case by case**. Assess the specific customer, apply enhanced measures where needed, and exit only when risk cannot be managed within appetite, for example when a customer refuses to provide essential information or keeps generating unexplained activity.

**Simplified due diligence (SDD)** is the other side of the RBA. Where risk is genuinely low, such as basic accounts with low balance and transaction limits designed for financial inclusion, regulations allow lighter identification and verification measures. SDD is still due diligence: the customer is still identified, screened and monitored. It is never allowed where there is suspicion of ML/TF or where specific higher-risk factors apply.

Pakistan has built tiered account and wallet structures so that low-income customers can open accounts easily with limits that keep risk low. When limits are exceeded, fuller due diligence is required before the customer moves to a higher tier.

cards.question: After a news story about charity fraud, a bank's sales head proposes closing every NPO account. What is the strongest objection under the risk-based approach?
options: NPO accounts are exempt from AML/CFT requirements
Blanket exits are de-risking: each NPO should be assessed and managed individually, with exit only when risk cannot be managed
The bank must keep all NPO accounts whatever their risk
Only SECP can decide whether an NPO may hold a bank account
cards.explanation: The RBA calls for case-by-case assessment. Blanket exits harm legitimate charities and push funds into unmonitored channels. NPOs are not exempt, and banks can exit individual relationships whose risk cannot be managed.

cards.title: Make the assessment useful, not decorative
cards.body: An enterprise risk assessment that runs to 200 pages but cites no data, is not updated after a major new product, and is unknown to branch managers will not impress an inspector. Keep the main findings short, data-based and linked to actions with owners and deadlines. Share a one-page summary with branches so they know the top risks in their area.

cards.question: Which customer should NOT receive simplified due diligence, even though she holds a low-limit basic account?
options: A domestic worker in Rawalpindi whose small monthly salary is credited by her employer
A student whose low-limit account received transfers from twenty unrelated people in one week and was emptied the same day
A retired schoolteacher receiving a pension
A small shopkeeper using the account for occasional utility bill payments
cards.explanation: Simplified measures are never appropriate where there are indicators of ML/TF. Many unrelated incoming transfers emptied immediately is a classic money mule pattern requiring review, escalation and possibly an STR. The other customers show activity consistent with a low-risk profile.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: The RBA puts stronger controls where risk is higher and simpler ones where risk is genuinely lower; it is never permission to skip core obligations.
Inherent risk minus effective controls gives residual risk, which must fit the board-approved risk appetite.
The enterprise risk assessment uses internal data and the national risk assessment, covers ML, TF and PF, and is refreshed when things change.
Customer, product, geography and channel factors combine; assess them together, not in isolation.
Ratings must drive action and be re-rated on triggers; overrides need reasons and approval.
De-risking whole categories is not risk management; assess case by case and use SDD only where risk is truly low and there is no suspicion.

cards.prompt: Pick one product or customer segment you deal with. What makes it risky, which controls actually reduce that risk today, and is there one control you suspect looks good on paper but would fail if tested?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes 'residual risk'?
options: The risk created by customers who were onboarded before the current policy and have not yet been reviewed
The risk that exists before any controls are applied
The risk that remains after controls have been applied, to be compared with risk appetite
The risk that the regulator will impose a monetary penalty after finding weaknesses during an on-site inspection
quiz.explanation: Residual risk is what remains once controls are applied, and it is compared with the board-approved risk appetite. Risk before controls is inherent risk. Legacy customers and penalty risk are separate concepts.

quiz.question: A microfinance bank is preparing its enterprise-wide risk assessment. Which input is most important to include from outside the institution?
options: Pakistan's national risk assessment and relevant FMU and FATF typologies
Competitor banks' marketing brochures
The bank's annual profit forecast, so that risk ratings stay aligned with business growth targets
Customer satisfaction survey results
quiz.explanation: The national risk assessment and typologies tell the institution which threats are most relevant in Pakistan and how criminals operate. Profit forecasts, brochures and satisfaction surveys say nothing about ML/TF/PF threats.

quiz.question: Mehwish, a relationship manager, asks compliance to downgrade a wealthy property developer from high to medium risk because 'he is a respected family and EDD annoys him'. The customer's risk factors have not changed. What should compliance do?
options: Approve the downgrade because relationship managers know their clients best
Approve it temporarily and review after six months
Downgrade the rating to medium but quietly keep collecting the full EDD file in case of a future inspection
Refuse: an override needs a documented risk-based reason, and social standing or customer inconvenience is not one
quiz.explanation: Overrides must be justified by risk factors, documented and approved. Social standing and customer annoyance do not reduce ML/TF risk, and downgrading to avoid EDD is a recognised control failure. A temporary or cosmetic downgrade has the same flaw.

quiz.question: Which situation best illustrates delivery channel risk?
options: A customer who is a domestic PEP
A wallet provider relying on paid agents to onboard customers in remote areas
A customer sending money from Pakistan to a country that is subject to UN Security Council sanctions
A business customer dealing in used cars
quiz.explanation: Channel risk concerns how customers are reached and served. Reliance on paid agents adds risk because the institution depends on a third party's diligence and incentives. PEP status and business type are customer factors; the sanctioned country is a geographic factor.

quiz.question: A bank launches a new instant international transfer feature in its mobile app. What does FATF expect before launch?
options: An assessment of the ML/TF risks of the new product and appropriate controls to manage them
Approval from the FMU for the product design
Nothing further, provided every existing customer who will use the feature has already completed full CDD
A commitment to file a currency transaction report with the FMU for every international transfer made through the app
quiz.explanation: New products, practices and technologies must be risk-assessed before launch, with controls to manage the identified risks. The FMU does not approve products, existing CDD does not cover new product risks, and CTRs relate to cash transactions.

quiz.question: Faisal Awan, a customer rated low risk two years ago, has just been elected to a provincial assembly. What should happen to his risk rating?
options: It stays low until the next scheduled periodic review, when his new public role can be considered alongside other changes
It changes only if he starts transacting in cash
It should be reassessed now, because becoming a PEP is a trigger event requiring immediate re-rating and enhanced measures
It is automatically closed because PEPs cannot hold accounts
quiz.explanation: Becoming a PEP is a trigger for immediate re-rating rather than waiting for the scheduled review. PEPs can hold accounts subject to enhanced measures; cash activity is not the only reason to reassess.

quiz.question: Which statement about simplified due diligence (SDD) is correct?
options: SDD means the customer does not need to be identified
SDD may apply to genuinely lower-risk situations but never where there is suspicion of ML/TF
SDD applies automatically to all customers who have banked with the institution for more than five years
SDD allows sanctions screening to be skipped for low-value accounts
quiz.explanation: SDD lightens some measures where risk is demonstrably low, but customers are still identified, screened and monitored, and SDD is ruled out when suspicion arises. Length of relationship does not on its own justify SDD.

quiz.question: A bank's AML team finds that its enterprise risk assessment was last updated four years ago, before the bank launched wallets and trade finance for SMEs. What is the main weakness?
options: The assessment should have been prepared by the external auditor
The assessment only needs to be updated when SBP specifically requests it during an inspection or thematic review
Wallets and SME trade finance are low-risk products, so the existing assessment did not need to be updated for them
The assessment no longer reflects the bank's actual risks, so controls may not match them
quiz.explanation: Material changes such as new products must trigger an update, otherwise monitoring, CDD and training are calibrated to an outdated risk picture. Management owns the assessment, not the external auditor, and wallets and trade finance carry significant risks.

quiz.question: Why does FATF warn against wholesale de-risking of sectors such as exchange companies or charities?
options: It can push activity into unregulated channels and exclude legitimate users, without managing the actual risk involved
Because these sectors are legally exempt from AML/CFT controls
Because banks must accept every customer who presents a valid CNIC
Because de-risking sharply increases the number of defensive STRs filed by banks, overloading the FMU's analysts
quiz.explanation: Blanket exits drive money into unmonitored channels such as hawala and harm financial inclusion and humanitarian work, while doing nothing to assess actual risk. These sectors are not exempt, and banks can decline individual customers whose risk is unmanageable.

quiz.question: Which of these is outside any acceptable risk appetite, rather than simply 'high risk'?
options: A foreign PEP with a well-documented source of wealth
A shell bank seeking a correspondent account
A jeweller with heavy cash turnover
A non-resident Pakistani opening an account through a digital channel
quiz.explanation: Shell banks have no physical presence and no meaningful supervision, and correspondent relationships with them are prohibited. PEPs, jewellers and non-resident customers can be accepted with appropriate, sometimes enhanced, due diligence.

sessions.title: Customer Due Diligence: Knowing Who Is Really There
sessions.summary: Every relationship passes through the gatehouse. Learn to identify and verify customers, find the natural persons behind companies and trusts, choose between simplified, standard and enhanced measures, and handle PEPs, NPOs, correspondent relationships and record keeping.
objectives: List the elements of customer due diligence and when it must be performed
Identify and verify individuals and legal persons using Pakistani documents and NADRA verification
Trace beneficial ownership through layered structures to the natural persons who own or control them
Apply enhanced due diligence to PEPs, NPOs, correspondent banking and other higher-risk relationships
Explain what records must be kept, why, and what to do when CDD cannot be completed

cards.title: The four elements of CDD
cards.body:
**Customer due diligence (CDD)** is how an institution knows who it is dealing with and what to expect from them. FATF and Pakistani regulations describe four core elements:

1. **Identify the customer and verify** that identity using reliable, independent sources.
2. **Identify the beneficial owner** and take reasonable, risk-based measures to verify who that person is, so that you know which natural persons ultimately own or control the customer.
3. **Understand the purpose and intended nature** of the relationship: what the account will be used for, expected volumes, sources of funds, main counterparties and countries.
4. **Conduct ongoing due diligence**: monitor transactions against that understanding and keep CDD information up to date.

**When CDD is required:**

- when establishing a business relationship
- when carrying out occasional transactions above thresholds set in regulations, including certain wire transfers
- whenever there is a **suspicion of ML/TF**, regardless of any threshold or exemption
- when there are doubts about the accuracy of previously obtained information

**People acting on behalf of the customer**, such as signatories, attorneys and authorised persons, must also be identified and verified, and their authority checked.

**Timing.** Verification should normally be completed before the relationship is established. Regulations allow limited flexibility in some low-risk cases, but the risk must be managed, for example by restricting the account until verification is complete.

CDD is not just a form. The 'purpose and nature' element is what makes monitoring possible: without a clear expected profile, there is no way to tell whether later activity is unusual.

cards.title: Identification and verification in Pakistan
cards.body:
**Individuals.** For Pakistani citizens, the main identity document is the NADRA-issued **CNIC** or **SNIC**; overseas Pakistanis may use a **NICOP**. Foreign nationals are generally identified with a passport and valid visa or other permission to stay, and other NADRA-issued cards such as the Pakistan Origin Card apply in specific cases. Always check the document's validity and expiry and follow your institution's instructions on expired identity documents.

**Verification tools:**

- **NADRA biometric verification** at branches and through approved devices confirms that the person standing in front of you is the person on the card.
- **NADRA verification services** such as Verisys confirm the CNIC data against NADRA's records.
- Digital onboarding uses approved remote verification methods set by SBP for the relevant account type.

**Legal persons and arrangements** need documents that prove existence, ownership, control and authority, for example:

- **Companies:** certificate of incorporation, memorandum and articles, list of directors, board resolution authorising the account and signatories, beneficial ownership information, and the identity of directors and signatories.
- **Partnerships:** partnership deed, registration where applicable, identity of all partners.
- **Sole proprietors:** identity of the owner plus evidence that the business exists, such as tax registration, utility bills or a site visit.
- **Trusts, waqfs, societies and NPOs:** the constituting instrument, registration certificate, governing body members, and identity of key persons.

Remember to verify the **business**, not just the documents. A neat set of papers for a company with no premises, employees or customers should prompt questions, not reassurance.

cards.title: Biometrics confirm identity, not legitimacy
cards.body: A successful biometric match proves that the person is who the CNIC says. It does not prove that the money is clean, that the person is acting for themselves, or that their stated occupation is true. Money mules pass biometric checks every day. Use verification as the start of CDD, then ask the questions that build a real profile: occupation, income, purpose of the account, expected transactions.

cards.title: Beneficial ownership: finding the real person
cards.body:
The **beneficial owner** is the **natural person** (a human being, never a company) who ultimately owns or controls a customer, or on whose behalf a transaction is conducted. Criminals use companies, trusts and nominees precisely because they hide this person.

For legal persons, a **cascade** is used:

1. **Ownership:** identify natural persons who ultimately hold a controlling ownership interest, measured against a percentage threshold set in the regulations (commonly 25 percent in international practice; check the threshold in the current SBP or SECP regulations that apply to you). Look through every layer of corporate ownership.
2. **Control by other means:** if no one qualifies through ownership, or ownership does not reveal who controls, identify natural persons exercising control through other means, such as voting agreements, the power to appoint the board, or family arrangements.
3. **Senior managing official:** only if no natural person can be identified through steps 1 and 2, record the natural person holding the senior management position, and document what you did to get there.

For **trusts and similar arrangements**, identify the settlor, trustees, protector if any, beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and any other natural person exercising effective control.

**Sources of information** include the customer's own declarations, shareholder registers, company registry information including beneficial ownership information maintained with SECP, foreign registry extracts and reliable commercial databases. Verify on a risk basis: the more complex or higher-risk the structure, the more independent verification you need.

**Red flags:** nominee shareholders or directors without explanation, ownership through jurisdictions with secrecy laws, frequent ownership changes, circular ownership, and structures more complex than the business needs.

cards.title: Unwrapping a Karachi trading company
cards.body:
Indus Bright Trading (Pvt) Ltd, a newly formed Karachi company, applies for a current account and an import letter of credit facility. Its documents show:

- 60 percent of shares held by Crescent Holdings FZE, a company in a Gulf free zone
- 40 percent held by Mr Arif Soomro, a Karachi resident who is also the sole director
- Crescent Holdings is wholly owned by a trust registered in an offshore jurisdiction

Asad Rind, the onboarding analyst, works through the cascade.

**Ownership.** Mr Soomro holds 40 percent directly, so he is a beneficial owner. For the 60 percent, Asad asks for Crescent's registry extract and the trust deed. The trust deed shows that the settlor is Mr Tariq Jadoon, a Lahore businessman, the trustee is a professional trust company, and the beneficiaries are Mr Jadoon's children.

**Control.** The trust deed gives Mr Jadoon the power to replace the trustee and direct investments. That gives him effective control of 60 percent of the company.

**Findings.** The beneficial owners are Mr Soomro (40 percent, director) and Mr Jadoon (controller of the 60 percent through the trust). Mr Jadoon's children, as beneficiaries, are also identified. Screening shows that Mr Jadoon was a senior official of a public sector corporation until two years ago, making him a domestic PEP to assess further.

**Decision.** The relationship is rated high risk. Asad requests the source of wealth for Mr Jadoon, the rationale for the offshore structure, and trade references. Senior management approval is sought before opening.

If the customer had refused to explain who controls the trust, the right answer would have been to decline the relationship and consider whether an STR was needed.

cards.question: A company's shares are held in many small stakes, none of which reaches the ownership threshold, and nobody appears to exercise control by other means. Whom should the bank record as beneficial owner?
options: The company itself, since it is the legal owner of its assets
The largest corporate shareholder
The natural person holding the senior managing position, with the steps taken documented
No one; the field can be left blank
cards.explanation: The cascade ends with the senior managing official when no natural person qualifies through ownership or control. The beneficial owner must always be a natural person, so neither the company nor a corporate shareholder can be recorded, and leaving it blank is a CDD failure.

cards.title: Simplified, standard and enhanced due diligence
cards.body:
The depth of CDD follows the risk rating.

**Simplified due diligence (SDD)** applies only where risk is demonstrably low and regulations permit it, for example limited-function basic accounts with low limits. It may involve fewer documents or less frequent updates. It is never allowed where there is suspicion of ML/TF or specific higher-risk scenarios.

**Standard CDD** applies to most customers: full identification and verification, beneficial ownership, purpose and nature, screening and ongoing monitoring.

**Enhanced due diligence (EDD)** applies to higher-risk customers and to categories where regulations require it, such as foreign PEPs, correspondent relationships and customers linked to high-risk jurisdictions identified by FATF. EDD measures include:

- **Source of funds:** where the money for this relationship or transaction comes from (for example, the sale of a property, a salary, business proceeds).
- **Source of wealth:** how the customer built their overall wealth (for example, a family textile business, a long career abroad). This is different from source of funds and matters most for PEPs and wealthy clients.
- **Senior management approval** to open or continue the relationship.
- **More information** about the business, its counterparties and expected activity, with independent corroboration such as financial statements, tax returns or site visits.
- **Enhanced ongoing monitoring**: lower thresholds, more frequent reviews and closer scrutiny of unusual transactions.

**Customers from high-risk jurisdictions.** For countries FATF calls on members to apply enhanced measures or countermeasures to, EDD is required, and some regulations specify additional steps. Check the current FATF lists and SBP or SECP instructions after each FATF plenary.

The quality of EDD is judged by whether the answers make sense. A source-of-wealth note saying only 'business' is not EDD.

cards.title: Politically exposed persons
cards.body:
A **politically exposed person (PEP)** is someone who is or has been entrusted with a prominent public function. Their position gives them access to public funds and decisions, which creates corruption risk.

**Categories:**

- **Foreign PEPs:** prominent public functions in another country.
- **Domestic PEPs:** prominent functions in Pakistan, for example federal and provincial ministers, members of parliament and provincial assemblies, senior judges, senior military officers, senior civil servants, heads of state-owned enterprises and important political party officials.
- **International organisation PEPs:** senior management of international organisations.

Middle-ranking or junior officials are not PEPs by definition, although they may still be higher risk for other reasons.

**Family members and close associates** of PEPs are treated as PEPs for due diligence purposes, because they are often used to hold corrupt assets. Close associates include business partners and people known to have close personal or business ties.

**Measures.** Under FATF standards, foreign PEPs always require enhanced measures: senior management approval, establishing source of wealth and source of funds, and enhanced ongoing monitoring. For domestic and international organisation PEPs, the same measures apply when the relationship is assessed as higher risk. Pakistan's regulations set out how PEPs must be treated; check whether your regulator requires enhanced measures for all PEPs in your sector.

**When does PEP status end?** FATF's approach is risk-based rather than a fixed time limit. A former minister may still carry significant risk years after leaving office. Your institution's policy should set how declassification decisions are made and approved.

Being a PEP is not a crime. The aim is to make sure the PEP's money matches their legitimate income and wealth.

cards.title: The minister's brother-in-law
cards.body:
Bilal Shah, a building materials supplier in Peshawar, has banked with a branch for ten years as a medium-risk customer with turnover of around PKR 8 million a month. In the past four months turnover has risen to PKR 60 million, mostly from payments by contractors working on provincial road projects.

A local news report mentions that Bilal's sister is married to the newly appointed provincial minister for communications and works.

**What the compliance team does:**

1. **Identifies the PEP link.** Bilal is a family member of a domestic PEP (brother-in-law through marriage). The branch's screening had not picked this up because the minister was appointed after Bilal's last review.
2. **Re-rates** Bilal as high risk and applies EDD.
3. **Asks for an explanation** of the turnover increase, copies of supply contracts, and the identity of the contractors paying him.
4. **Reviews the pattern.** Several contractors paying him were awarded contracts by the minister's department. Some payments are round amounts unrelated to invoices, and Bilal transfers large sums onward to a property developer.
5. **Seeks senior management approval** to continue the relationship under enhanced monitoring, and the compliance officer considers whether the facts give reasonable grounds to suspect that the payments are disguised kickbacks.

The compliance officer concludes that suspicion exists and files an STR. The branch continues normal service while compliance decides on the relationship, and no one tells Bilal about the report.

**Lesson:** PEP risk often sits with relatives and associates, and it appears in the middle of a relationship, not just at onboarding.

cards.question: Which customer is a PEP for due diligence purposes under the FATF standards?
options: A grade-17 officer in a district education office
The spouse of a sitting federal minister
A businessman who donated to several political parties
A retired schoolteacher who once stood unsuccessfully in a local election
cards.explanation: Family members of PEPs are treated as PEPs for due diligence purposes. Middle-ranking officials are not PEPs by definition, and donors or unsuccessful candidates are not PEPs merely for that, although other risk factors may still apply.

cards.title: NPOs, correspondent banking and other higher-risk relationships
cards.body:
**Non-profit organisations.** Charities and NPOs do vital work in Pakistan, from flood relief to education, but some have been abused for terrorist financing, for example by proscribed groups operating through new front names. FATF expects a targeted, risk-based approach that does not disrupt legitimate charity. Good NPO due diligence covers:

- registration status and the authority with which the NPO is registered
- governing body members and key officials, all screened against sanctions and proscription lists
- sources of funds, especially foreign donations and large cash collections
- how and where funds are used, including areas of operation and implementing partners
- financial statements and internal controls

Red flags include funds sent to areas unrelated to stated projects, office bearers linked to proscribed organisations, large cash withdrawals with no clear purpose, and collection drives in the name of a banned group's known causes.

**Correspondent banking.** When a Pakistani bank provides accounts to foreign banks, or relies on foreign correspondents, it must assess the respondent's business, reputation, quality of supervision and AML/CFT controls; obtain senior management approval; understand each party's responsibilities; and take extra care with payable-through accounts and nested relationships, where other banks use the respondent's account. Relationships with **shell banks** are prohibited, and respondents must not allow shell banks to use their accounts.

**Wire transfers.** Originator and beneficiary information must travel with cross-border and domestic transfers as regulations specify. Missing information is a reason to investigate, and possibly reject or suspend the transfer.

**Money service businesses.** Exchange companies and payment providers banking with a bank must hold valid licences and be assessed like any higher-risk financial institution customer.

cards.title: Record keeping and incomplete CDD
cards.body:
**Why records matter.** The FMU and law enforcement can only follow the money if institutions can reconstruct transactions and show who was behind them. Inspectors also judge your compliance largely from your records.

**What to keep:**

- CDD records: identity documents, verification results, beneficial ownership information, account files, business correspondence and the results of any analysis
- transaction records sufficient to reconstruct individual transactions, including amounts, currencies, dates, parties and accounts
- internal reports of suspicion, the compliance decision and its reasons, and copies of STRs and CTRs filed
- screening results and how potential matches were resolved

**How long.** FATF sets a minimum of five years. Pakistan's law and regulations require records to be kept for longer, at least ten years for the main categories, counted from points such as the end of the relationship or the date of the transaction. Confirm the exact periods and starting points in the current AMLA provisions and your regulator's regulations, and keep records longer where an investigation or court case is ongoing.

**Availability.** Records must be retrievable quickly when lawfully requested. A record that exists only in a branch storeroom in boxes nobody can search does not meet the standard.

**When CDD cannot be completed.** If you cannot identify the customer, verify their identity, identify the beneficial owner or understand the purpose of the relationship:

- do not open the account or carry out the transaction
- for an existing relationship, consider terminating it in line with policy
- **consider filing an STR**, because the refusal or inability may itself be suspicious

If you suspect ML/TF and believe that continuing CDD would tip off the customer, the standards allow you to stop the CDD process and file an STR instead.

cards.question: A prospective corporate customer refuses to name the natural persons behind its foreign parent company, saying 'our investors value privacy'. What should the bank do?
options: Open the account but rate it high risk
Accept a declaration that no beneficial owner exceeds the threshold
Not open the account, and consider whether an STR is warranted
Open the account with a low transaction limit until the owners are disclosed
cards.explanation: Beneficial ownership is a core CDD element. If it cannot be established, the relationship should not be opened, and the refusal may itself be suspicious. A high rating or a limit does not cure missing CDD, and an unverified declaration contradicted by the customer's own refusal is not reliable.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: CDD has four elements: identify and verify the customer, identify the beneficial owner, understand purpose and nature, and monitor on an ongoing basis.
Biometric and NADRA verification confirm identity; they do not confirm legitimacy or source of funds.
The beneficial owner is always a natural person; use the ownership, control and senior managing official cascade and document each step.
EDD means real answers on source of funds and wealth, senior management approval and closer monitoring, not just extra forms.
PEP risk extends to family members and close associates and can arise mid-relationship.
If CDD cannot be completed, do not proceed and consider an STR. Keep records retrievable for the full legal retention period.

cards.prompt: Recall a customer file you have seen that looked complete but told you little about what the customer actually does or where their money comes from. What two questions would have turned it into a genuinely useful CDD file?

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the core elements of customer due diligence?
options: Identifying and verifying the customer
Identifying the beneficial owner
Understanding the purpose and intended nature of the relationship
Obtaining the customer's written consent before any STR is filed
quiz.explanation: The core elements are identification and verification, beneficial ownership, purpose and nature, and ongoing monitoring. Customer consent has no role in STR filing; telling the customer about an STR would be tipping off.
