bank.question: A payment fintech wants to raise wallet limits for customers onboarded through agents, without stronger verification, to grow volumes before year end. The compliance head objects. Which argument is strongest under the RBA?
options: Higher limits raise mule risk, so they should rise only with stronger verification and monitoring
Higher limits are always prohibited for wallets
Only the FMU can approve changes to wallet limits
Agent-onboarded customers must always be rated high risk regardless of controls, so higher limits would breach policy
bank.explanation: The RBA links risk-increasing changes to matching controls. Higher limits for weakly verified, agent-onboarded wallets increase mule and fraud exposure. Tiered limits are allowed within regulatory rules, the FMU does not approve product limits, and blanket high ratings would ignore controls.

bank.question: A bank's analysis shows that 80 percent of its STRs relate to accounts opened through one digital channel, while the enterprise risk assessment rates that channel as low risk. What should happen?
options: Nothing until the next scheduled annual update
The STRs should first be reviewed for defensive filing, because the channel has been rated low risk
The channel should be closed immediately
The channel's risk rating and controls should be reassessed in light of the evidence
bank.explanation: Internal data such as STR concentrations is a key input, and a significant mismatch is a trigger to revisit the assessment and controls. Waiting ignores evidence, assuming defensive filing reverses the logic, and immediate closure is premature before analysis.

bank.question: A wealthy client of a bank's priority banking unit is rated high risk. The unit head proposes reducing EDD reviews to once every three years 'to improve client experience'. Which response is correct?
options: Approve, provided the client signs an annual self-declaration confirming that his circumstances have not changed
Refuse: review frequency follows the risk rating, and client convenience is not a risk reason
Approve, because review frequency is a commercial decision
Downgrade the client to medium so that the longer cycle applies
bank.explanation: Review frequency is tied to risk under policy, and changes need risk-based justification. A self-declaration does not replace EDD, and downgrading to reach a preferred review cycle is a classic improper override.

bank.question: Under the risk-based approach, which obligation applies regardless of a customer's low risk rating?
options: Obtaining source of wealth evidence, because every customer's total net worth must be understood under the RBA
Senior management approval at onboarding
Sanctions and proscription screening, and reporting suspicion if it arises
Annual site visits
bank.explanation: Low risk can justify lighter CDD, but sanctions screening and reporting suspicion are never switched off. Source of wealth, senior management approval and site visits are enhanced measures that apply to higher-risk relationships.

bank.question: A bank exits all accounts of licensed exchange companies after a single exchange company is fined, even those with strong controls and clean histories. A year later, the bank notices a rise in unexplained cash and transfers linked to informal money transfer in its retail accounts. What best explains this?
options: Exchange companies are unregulated in Pakistan, so exiting them made no difference
The FMU stopped receiving STRs from exchange companies
The rise is unrelated, because informal transfer never uses bank accounts
Blanket de-risking pushed legitimate flows into informal channels that now pass unseen through retail accounts
bank.explanation: FATF warns that de-risking can drive activity into less transparent channels. Exchange companies are licensed and supervised by SBP, and informal transfer frequently uses ordinary accounts to settle balances. The exit removed visibility without managing the underlying risk.

bank.question: Which situation best justifies a documented downward override of a model-generated 'high' rating?
options: A state-owned utility whose large volumes are normal for its role, with transparent ownership and no adverse information
A jeweller who complains that EDD questions are intrusive
A PEP whose relationship manager has known him and his family personally for more than twenty years without issue
A customer who promises to reduce cash deposits next year
bank.explanation: An override is justified when the model misreads genuine risk, such as volumes that are normal for a state-owned utility with transparent ownership, and the reasoning is documented and approved. Complaints, personal familiarity and promises are not risk-based reasons.

bank.question: A private limited company applies for an account. Its shareholders are Ms Sara (20 percent), Mr Omar (20 percent) and a Dubai company (60 percent) wholly owned by Mr Khalid, a Lahore businessman, who also has the right to appoint all the Pakistani company's directors. Ms Sara and Mr Omar are unrelated to him and to each other. Assuming a 25 percent threshold applies, who is the beneficial owner?
options: Ms Sara and Mr Omar, because they are the only individuals holding shares directly
Mr Khalid, who owns 60 percent through the Dubai company and controls board appointments
The Dubai company, because it holds the majority of the shares
Nobody, because no individual holds 25 percent or more of the Pakistani company's shares directly in their own name
bank.explanation: Ownership must be traced through intermediate companies to natural persons: Mr Khalid ultimately owns 60 percent and also controls the board, so he is the beneficial owner. Ms Sara and Mr Omar are below the threshold and have no stated control, though they are still identified as shareholders. A company can never be a beneficial owner.

bank.question: A sole proprietor running an electronics shop in Rawalpindi presents a CNIC that passes biometric verification, a tax registration certificate and a rent agreement. His expected turnover is PKR 40 million a month, far above similar shops. What is the best CDD approach?
options: Accept the documents, since they are valid and verified, and set the expected turnover at the level the customer declared
Refuse the account, because sole proprietors are not permitted to have turnover above that of comparable shops in the area
Verify the business itself, such as by site visit and sales evidence, before agreeing a profile
Open the account and file a CTR on the first deposit
bank.explanation: Documents prove existence on paper; an implausible turnover requires verifying the business and understanding the source of funds before setting the profile. Accepting the declared figure would make later monitoring meaningless, refusing outright is not risk-based, and a CTR is unrelated to onboarding judgement.

bank.question: A customer wants to open an account with an expired CNIC, saying he has applied for renewal and shows the NADRA token. What is the best approach for staff?
options: Open the account normally, since the CNIC number stays the same after renewal and NADRA has issued a token
Ask the customer to open the account in a relative's name until renewal
Refuse service permanently
Follow the bank's current procedure and SBP instructions on expired identity documents
bank.explanation: Expired identity documents are covered by specific regulatory instructions and institutional procedures, and staff must follow them rather than improvise. Opening normally ignores the rules, using a relative's name creates a false account holder, and permanent refusal is disproportionate.

bank.question: Which customer most clearly requires enhanced due diligence under the FATF standards, regardless of the institution's own risk scoring?
options: A foreign PEP, such as a serving minister of another country, opening a personal account with a bank in Pakistan
A Pakistani software house receiving payments from overseas clients
A domestic PEP whose relationship has been assessed as standard risk after the bank's review of his profile
A salaried employee of a multinational company in Karachi
bank.explanation: FATF requires enhanced measures for foreign PEPs in all cases. For domestic PEPs, enhanced measures apply when the relationship is assessed as higher risk, unless local regulations require more. The software house and the employee require EDD only if risk factors justify it.

bank.question: A domestic PEP's adult son opens an account and receives PKR 30 million from his father described as a 'gift' for buying a house. What is the most important EDD question?
options: Whether the son has a valid email address for statements
Whether the house is in a gated community
How the father built the wealth used for the gift, and whether it fits his known income
Whether the son already holds another bank account where he could have received the gift instead
bank.explanation: Family members of PEPs are treated as PEPs, and a large gift from the PEP makes the father's source of wealth central to judging corruption risk. The other questions do not address whether the funds could be proceeds of corruption.

bank.question: A Lahore-registered NPO running flood relief in Sindh asks to receive large foreign donations. Its trustees screen clean, but the bank cannot find out which local partners actually distribute aid. What is the most proportionate response?
options: Ask about implementing partners and the use of funds, monitor closely, and then decide on accepting the foreign inflows
Close the account, because NPOs receiving large foreign donations fall outside any reasonable risk appetite
Accept the inflows without further questions, because humanitarian work is exempt from CDD
Accept the inflows but cap each donation at a small amount
bank.explanation: FATF expects targeted, risk-based measures for NPOs: understanding how and through whom funds are used, with enhanced monitoring where needed. Blanket exits harm legitimate charities, humanitarian work is not exempt, and an arbitrary cap does not address the missing information.

bank.question: A foreign respondent bank asks a Pakistani bank to open a USD correspondent account. The respondent says several smaller banks in its region will also use the account to make payments. What is the key additional risk and response?
options: There is no added risk, because the respondent bank is licensed and supervised in its home country, which covers its users
Nested use: understand which banks will use the account and their controls, and restrict if needed
The only issue is currency risk, which treasury should manage
The Pakistani bank should file a CTR on every payment through the account
bank.explanation: Nested relationships let other banks access the correspondent indirectly, so the Pakistani bank must understand who they are and assess their controls, and may limit or decline the arrangement. Home regulation of the respondent does not cover nested banks, and CTRs concern cash transactions.

bank.question: A domestic outward wire transfer arrives at the bank's payment desk with the originator's name but no account number or unique reference, and the originator details cannot be completed. What should the bank do?
options: Process it, because originator information requirements only apply to cross-border wire transfers, not domestic ones
Process it and complete the missing details from guesswork
Return it automatically and take no further action
Follow the policy on incomplete transfers, such as requesting data or rejecting, and consider suspicion
bank.explanation: Wire transfer rules require originator and beneficiary information to accompany transfers as regulations specify. Missing information calls for a risk-based decision under policy, and may itself be a red flag worth assessing for an STR. Processing without it or inventing data breaches the rules, and automatic return without assessment misses the suspicion question.

bank.question: A relationship manager writes the source of wealth for a high-risk client as 'business'. In a review, which improvement would make this acceptable EDD?
options: Adding the words 'family business, established' to show the wealth comes from a long-running enterprise
Obtaining the client's signature on the note
Explaining what the business is, how the wealth accumulated over time, and what independent evidence supports it
Asking the branch manager to countersign the note
bank.explanation: EDD must produce a plausible, evidence-based explanation of how wealth was built. Signatures and countersignatures add approval but not substance, and adding vague words does not create understanding.

bank.question: During a periodic review, a bank discovers that a corporate customer's ownership changed eight months ago: a new foreign holding company now owns 70 percent. The customer never informed the bank. What should the bank do?
options: Nothing, because the account was opened with complete CDD
Identify, verify and screen the new beneficial owners, re-rate the customer and consider why the change was not disclosed
Freeze the account immediately under the sanctions rules until the new foreign owners have been identified
Note the change for the next review in three years
bank.explanation: Ongoing due diligence requires CDD to be updated when ownership changes, including identifying the new beneficial owners, screening and re-rating. A freeze applies to sanctions matches, not ownership changes, and deferring the update leaves unknown owners in place.

bank.question: An alert shows that a garment retailer in Lahore deposited cash of about PKR 1.8 million every working day for two weeks before Eid, matching the same pattern in the previous three years, with no transfers to unusual parties. What is the most appropriate outcome?
options: Close it with a rationale citing the seasonal pattern, prior years and normal counterparties
File an STR, because daily cash deposits of that size are always suspicious regardless of the customer's history
Close the alert with the single word 'seasonal', since the pattern is obvious from the dates of the deposits
Escalate to the FMU for its view before closing
bank.explanation: The activity matches a documented seasonal pattern, so the alert can be closed with a specific rationale referencing the evidence. Filing an STR without grounds is defensive filing, a one-word note is inadequate, and the FMU does not advise on individual alerts.

bank.question: An importer of mobile phone accessories in Karachi pays a supplier in East Asia against invoices whose unit prices are about three times higher than the same importer's previous shipments of identical items. Customs declarations show the lower historical values. What is the most likely concern?
options: Under-invoicing of imports to reduce the customs duty payable, which is a tax matter rather than an AML concern
A normal price increase that needs no review
Phantom shipment, because the goods were declared to customs
Over-invoicing to move excess value out of Pakistan, possibly combined with customs fraud
bank.explanation: Paying the supplier far more than the declared value suggests over-invoicing in the banking documents to move value abroad, while lower customs values point to duty evasion. A tripling of price for identical goods needs explanation, and the goods physically arrived, so this is not a phantom shipment.

bank.question: A branchless banking agent in a small town processes ten times more cash-in and cash-out transactions than nearby agents, many for the same few wallet accounts. What is the most likely risk?
options: The agent is simply more popular, thanks to good customer service and a convenient location near the market
The wallet accounts are dormant
The agent may be running informal money transfer or facilitating mule activity through the wallets
The agent is under-reporting cash for tax purposes, which is a matter for the tax authorities rather than the bank
bank.explanation: Volumes far above peers concentrated on a few wallets suggest the agent may be moving money for others, such as hawala-style transfers or mule networks. Popularity would show many different customers, not a few heavily used wallets.

bank.question: A compliance officer is drafting an STR narrative. Which version is most useful to the FMU?
options: 'Customer appears suspicious and may be involved in money laundering; please investigate.'

'Between 2 and 25 March, the account received 19 cash deposits of PKR 480,000 to 495,000 by eight third parties at branches in three cities, and within 48 hours transferred 92 percent onward to four individuals. The customer, profiled as a schoolteacher, could not explain the source.'
'Large cash deposits observed. Customer is high risk.'
'Customer is a criminal and is laundering drug money.'
bank.explanation: A useful narrative sets out facts: who, what, when, how and why the activity departs from the profile. Vague narratives give analysts nothing to work with, and accusations of guilt are inappropriate because the reporter's role is to describe grounds for suspicion, not to determine crime.

bank.question: A customer comes to deposit PKR 3 million in cash. When the teller asks the routine source-of-funds question, he takes the cash back and leaves without depositing. There are earlier unexplained cash deposits on his account. What should happen?
options: Nothing, because no transaction took place
File a CTR for the attempted deposit, since the amount was above the threshold when presented at the counter
Call the customer to ask why he left
Escalate internally: an attempted transaction can be reported if there are grounds for suspicion
bank.explanation: STR obligations cover attempted transactions, and abandoning a deposit when asked about the source, combined with earlier unexplained deposits, should be escalated. CTRs relate to completed cash transactions, and calling him to ask why he left risks signalling suspicion.

bank.question: A bank files an STR on a business customer. Two weeks later, the customer requests a large trade loan. The credit team asks compliance whether it can approve. What is the best approach?
options: Decline the loan citing 'the STR filed on your account'
Assess it on risk, using the STR findings within the need-to-know group, without disclosure
Approve it automatically, because STRs must not affect business decisions
Ask the FMU for permission before deciding
bank.explanation: An STR is relevant to risk decisions, and the institution decides on the relationship on a risk basis, sharing information only with those who need it. Citing the STR is tipping off, ignoring it is imprudent, and the FMU does not approve lending decisions.

bank.question: A bank's CTR file contains many cash deposits where the depositor's CNIC was recorded incorrectly. Why is this a significant problem even though no suspicion is involved?
options: Inaccurate data weakens the FMU's ability to link cash activity with other intelligence
CTRs are only statistical and accuracy does not matter
Incorrect CNICs automatically convert each affected CTR into an STR that must then be investigated by the bank
CTRs containing errors must be deleted from the bank's records rather than corrected, to avoid misleading the FMU
bank.explanation: CTRs are valuable because the FMU can match them with STRs and other data, which depends on accurate identifiers. Data errors weaken intelligence and can be an inspection finding. Errors do not convert CTRs into STRs, and they should be corrected through the proper process, not deleted.

bank.question: An exchange company notices that a customer exchanges foreign currency for rupees almost daily with no trade or travel documents, then deposits the rupees into bank accounts of several unrelated businesses. He says he is a 'freelance consultant'. Which typology best fits?
options: Normal remittance activity by a freelancer
Trade finance fraud through letters of credit
Possible hawala or hundi settlement, converting and distributing value for others
Proliferation financing, because foreign currency is being converted repeatedly without trade documents
bank.explanation: Frequent undocumented currency conversion and distribution to unrelated businesses fits the settlement side of hawala or hundi, where an operator converts and moves value for others. Freelancers receive funds through documented channels, and there is no trade documentation or dual-use element to suggest trade fraud or PF.

bank.question: A victim reports an online investment scam, and the bank finds that the victim's transfer went to its own customer's account, from which most funds left by Raast transfers to five other banks within 20 minutes. What should the bank prioritise?
options: Act fast on fraud recall and inter-bank coordination, and escalate the receiving account for review as a possible mule
Wait for a police report and a court order before taking any action on the beneficiary account or the funds
Close the beneficiary account and tell the customer it was reported to the FMU
Treat it only as a customer service complaint
bank.explanation: Digital fraud moves fast, so recall and coordination must be immediate, and the receiving account's activity is a mule red flag requiring escalation and possibly an STR. Waiting loses funds, telling the customer about an FMU report is tipping off, and treating it as a complaint ignores the ML dimension.

bank.question: A teller sees a customer's brother-in-law, who works in the bank's IT department, viewing the customer's account in the system the day after the teller escalated a concern about it. What is the main concern?
options: None, because IT staff need access to all accounts
Only a general data privacy concern unrelated to AML, to be handled by the IT security team
That the teller made a mistake by escalating
A possible confidentiality breach risking tipping off, to be reported to compliance
bank.explanation: Information about escalations and STRs must be restricted to those who need it. A relative accessing the account without business need right after an escalation risks tipping off and should be reported for access review. Escalating was correct, and the issue goes beyond general privacy.

bank.question: A customer is a confirmed match to a person on NACTA's published list of proscribed persons. He holds a joint savings account with his wife, who is not listed. What should the bank do with the joint account?
options: Leave it open because the wife is not proscribed
Transfer the balance to the wife's individual account first, then freeze the now-empty joint account
Freeze it, because jointly held funds are covered, and refer any claim by the wife to compliance and the competent authority
Close the account and pay the balance in cash to the wife
bank.explanation: Freezing obligations cover funds owned or controlled jointly with others. Moving or paying out funds would make them available and defeat the freeze. The wife's legitimate claims can be raised through the competent authority, not resolved by the bank releasing funds.

bank.question: A screening analyst receives 400 potential matches after a list update. Under pressure, she bulk-clears all alerts with common first names such as 'Muhammad' without checking identifiers. What is the main risk?
options: True matches may be cleared, so a required freeze is missed
None, because alerts on very common names such as Muhammad are always false positives
Only the risk of a slower process
That the screening system will need to be reconfigured before any further alerts can be generated
bank.explanation: Bulk clearance without checking identifiers can release true matches, breaching TFS obligations. Designated persons often have common names, so name frequency is no basis for clearance. The answer is to tune matching and resource the team, not to skip verification.

bank.question: Which statement about the source of Pakistan's TFS obligations is correct?
options: UN designations apply in Pakistan only after the FMU has published them in its annual report and notified each bank
UN designations take effect through orders under the UN (Security Council) Act 1948; domestic proscription operates under the ATA 1997
Domestic proscription is made by SBP through circulars to banks
Only banks must comply with TFS; DNFBPs are exempt
bank.explanation: UN Security Council designations are implemented through orders under the UN (Security Council) Act 1948, and domestic proscription operates under the ATA. SBP passes instructions to its sector but does not proscribe, and TFS obligations extend beyond banks to everyone, including DNFBPs.

bank.question: A trade finance officer reviews an LC for 'precision CNC machine tools' bought by a newly formed Karachi trading firm for an end user in a third country. The applicant declines to provide end-use details, saying it is 'confidential'. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Process the LC, because CNC machine tools are not named on the UN list and the applicant is a registered company
Process the LC but charge a higher fee for the added risk
Reject the LC and tell the applicant it is suspected of proliferation
Escalate to compliance as a possible PF concern for checks on goods, parties and route
bank.explanation: CNC machine tools can be dual-use, and a new trading intermediary refusing end-use information is a PF red flag requiring escalation and checks. Goods need not be named on a list to be relevant, pricing does not address risk, and telling the applicant of suspicion risks tipping off.

bank.question: A frozen account belongs to a customer who has just been removed from the UN sanctions list. What should the bank do?
options: Keep the account frozen permanently as a precaution
Confirm the delisting and any other lists or orders, then unfreeze as officially instructed
Unfreeze the account only after the customer signs an indemnity protecting the bank from any future claims
Close the account and return funds by pay order without checks
bank.explanation: After delisting, funds should be released promptly in line with official instructions, once it is confirmed that the person is not still subject to another list, such as domestic proscription, or another legal order. Indefinite freezing has no legal basis, and an indemnity is not a substitute for proper checks.

bank.question: A branch manager receives an urgent instruction to freeze a newly designated customer's account at 4:30 pm on a Thursday, but decides to wait until Monday so he can 'inform the customer politely first'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, because freezes can wait until the next business week
Only that he should have informed the customer by letter rather than in person
Freezing must be immediate and without prior notice; both the delay and the warning breach this
Only that he should have asked the FMU for approval first
bank.explanation: TFS require immediate freezing without warning the designated person, who could otherwise move assets. Any delay and any prior notice defeat the purpose. The FMU does not approve freezes, and the method of notifying is irrelevant when prior notice is itself prohibited.

bank.question: A bank's compliance officer reports administratively to the head of retail banking, whose bonus depends on account growth, and has no direct access to the board. Several high-risk relationships were approved despite compliance objections. What is the most important remedy?
options: Give the compliance officer an independent reporting line with direct board access, real authority and adequate resources
Ask the head of retail to take more AML training
Increase the number of STRs filed to show stronger compliance
Move the compliance officer under internal audit so that audit can supervise and protect compliance decisions
bank.explanation: The compliance officer needs independence, authority and board access to resist business pressure. Training alone does not fix the conflict, inflating STRs is defensive filing, and putting compliance under audit compromises audit's independence as the third line.

bank.question: An insurer's board receives a quarterly AML report showing only 'policies issued' and 'STRs filed: 2'. What key information is the board missing to oversee the programme?
options: The names and account numbers of all customers on whom STRs were filed during the quarter, for board review
Details of every individual policy issued
Marketing results for new products
Risk-based MIS such as high-risk customer numbers, alert ageing, screening timeliness, training completion and open findings
bank.explanation: Boards need indicators showing whether controls are working: risk profile, backlogs, timeliness, training and open findings. Naming STR subjects to the board breaches need-to-know confidentiality, and individual policy details or marketing data do not show programme effectiveness.

bank.question: Following an SBP inspection, a bank receives a monetary penalty for AML/CFT breaches. The CEO asks whether the bank's staff can also face personal consequences. Which answer is accurate?
options: No, only the bank as an institution can be penalised, because staff act on its behalf and under its policies
Yes: staff may face disciplinary, regulatory and in some cases criminal consequences, depending on their role and conduct
Only the compliance officer can face consequences
Only staff who personally filed an STR can face consequences
bank.explanation: Individuals can face disciplinary action, regulatory action and, for offences such as tipping off or knowingly assisting laundering, criminal liability. Responsibility is not limited to the compliance officer, and good-faith STR filing is protected, not penalised.

bank.question: A bank's annual AML training is a 20-minute generic e-learning module for all staff, including trade finance officers and board members. An inspector criticises it. Which improvement best addresses the criticism?
options: Make the same module longer and add more slides and case studies so that it covers every role in the bank
Require staff to complete the module twice a year
Role-based training with local typologies, tests and records, tailored to each group
